reviews.reason: The repaired spectral-probability supplier now explicitly requires positive dimension. Here n is a positive integer, A_n is n-by-n Hermitian positive semidefinite, and x_n is a unit vector. F2 and proof 4.1 therefore retain their probability and tightness conclusions; neither the resolvent calculation nor the AC use changes.

The positive-dimension addition in the spectral-probability supplier is already satisfied by every positive n here. A_n is positive semidefinite and x_n is unit, so F3 and proof 4.1 still give probability measures and tightness. The bounded-entry consumer supplier remains unchanged, as do truncation and the explicit AC assumption.

Adding properness to strict propriety leaves F2, the expected logarithmic-loss definition, unchanged. Proof 4.1 uses the separately proved strict propriety of logarithmic loss to establish nonnegative KL and equality only at p=p*. The singleton action case is handled separately, and full support makes every displayed difference finite.

The supplier adds a bound only to its soft-influence regime. F2 and the iterated hard-depth-reduction proof use its unchanged general hard model, fixed end marker, earliest-max convention and length-independent maps. Neither the PARITY bit flip nor the one-type Dyck completion requires bounded initial states.

The repaired loss definition adds singleton measurability only in dimension one. This theorem explicitly assumes D>=2 and defines its objective by sample means on residual and boundary sets. F1 extends those weighted-square conventions to its measurable-set setting; F3 uses the higher-dimensional fill-distance branch. Neither exact finite-boundary masses nor the changed one-dimensional formula occurs.

The operator supplier now limits classical evaluation to existing finite flux derivatives. This theorem assumes a,b in C^{1,alpha} and evaluates C^2 functions, so all those derivatives exist by the product rule in proof 1.1. Its C^1 coefficients also justify the distributional divergence identity used in proofs 1.14-1.18. Positive sign, single b divergence, expanded coefficients, AC and CC remain consistent.

The finite global C^{1,alpha} assumptions on a,b and explicit C^2 trial-class requirement satisfy the repaired classical flux domain. Thus F3 and proof 1.1 retain the product-rule expansion and residual estimate. Proof 2.1 applies the zero-boundary existence/energy result to the error, without claiming individual H^1 membership for arbitrary nonzero boundary data.

The repaired parabolic supplier preserves classical existence and uniform residual stability used by F1 and proof 1.1. This consumer already states only energy convergence of errors in its exact-data branch. Proof 2.1 uses the separate zero-data energy-identification helper under explicit distributional compatibility; it never infers individual-function finite energy from Holder prescribed data. Hence the supplier correction requires no consumer change.

F2 now follows exactly from the corrected definition: properness supplies the pointwise minimizing inequality, and strict propriety adds uniqueness. Proof 1.1 integrates that inequality through the measurable posterior; proof 2.1 uses finite expected posterior risk to exclude infinity-minus-infinity before concluding almost-sure equality. AC and all kernel hypotheses remain explicit.

The Statement and Given require the one-symbol influence hypotheses, whose supplier explicitly uses addition of bounded token and positional embeddings. Thus the new combined-state bound follows by the triangle inequality. F2 uses only the unchanged end-marker convention; proof 4.1 realizes the sharp constant predictor with additive bounded states e_1, so sharpness is preserved.

The soft Statement explicitly combines uniformly bounded embeddings by addition, which already guarantees the supplier's new combined-state bound. Its parity and 2DYCK arguments invoke the corresponding one-symbol influence results in that regime. The hard branch uses the unchanged general hard model; the end marker and distinct stream/finite-word sampling laws are untouched.
